source.title_on_document: Generative AI as a cognitive support tool in early-stage design ideation: A human–AI co-ideation experiment

supplement.where: PLOS One Supporting information: S1-S5 Appendix (DOCX) and S1 Dataset (XLSX), listed on p. 22
supplement.holds: Rubrics and scoring anchors (S1, S2), questionnaire items (S3), task materials and prompts (S4), exploratory sequence-order analyses (S5), and the anonymized participant-level dataset with rater-level scores (S1 Dataset)

paper_design_summary: Thirty-two undergraduate design students in Taiwan each completed the same 60-minute product-design ideation task twice, once without AI and once with ChatGPT-4o and Midjourney v6, on separate class dates in a counterbalanced order. The order was assigned by participant number (P01-P16 human first, P17-P32 AI first) and the paper states it was not randomized. Three expert raters scored the ideation-process materials on six criteria and the final concept sheets on five design attributes, and participants rated their own experience.

studies.label: Counterbalanced within-subjects co-ideation experiment (temple-inspired cultural product design)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two conditions (human-only then AI-assisted, or AI-assisted then human-only); every participant completed both conditions
assignment.quote: Participants P01-P16 were assigned to the human-first sequence, whereas participants P17-P32 were assigned to the AI-first sequence. ... Sequence allocation was balanced but not randomized

arms.name: Human-only
arms.description: Individual ideation in three 20-minute stages (problem framing, idea exploration, selection) with keywords, mind maps, and sketches; no generative AI or other external ideation systems

arms.name: AI-assisted
arms.description: Same three 20-minute stages using ChatGPT-4o for text reframing and concept expansion and Midjourney v6 for visual exploration, after a 30-minute training session

participants.exclusions: None reported; all tests have 31 degrees of freedom, consistent with 32 participants in both conditions. No random assignment took place, so no randomized count exists.
participants.who: Undergraduate design students (mostly third-year, mean age 20.8) from a design department at a university in Taiwan; voluntary, no compensation or credit
participants.quote: A total of 32 undergraduate students were recruited from a design department at a university in Taiwan.
participants.locator: p. 5, Methods, Participants; t(31) in Tables 5-7, pp. 14-16

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4o and Midjourney v6 (public web versions)
ai_tool.how_used: ChatGPT-4o for interpreting and reframing the brief, generating textual concept directions, and refining prompts; Midjourney v6 for visual alternatives. Unrestricted prompt iteration with a structured prompt framework; selected Midjourney images could be kept in the concept sheet.

task.description: Design a temple-inspired cultural product for Gen Z users in Taiwan; produce ideation-process materials and one standardized concept sheet per condition
task.duration: 60 minutes of ideation per condition (three 20-minute stages), plus untimed concept-sheet assembly; conditions on separate class dates

outcomes.name: Creator perspective (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three expert raters (two senior design experts, one industry practitioner); rubric defines it as distinctiveness and originality of the participant's conceptualization; five-level anchors; raters' scores averaged per participant; Holm correction across six criteria; raters not fully blind to condition Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 3.55 (SD 0.491) vs AI M 4.03 (SD 0.435); t(31) = -5.066, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 0.90, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Innovation (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same three raters and procedure; rubric defines innovation as breakthrough potential and relevance to user or market needs (originality-related per the paper) Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 4.66 (SD 0.401) vs AI M 3.40 (SD 0.552); t(31) = 15.190, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 2.69, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Proposed solution strategies (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same three raters and procedure; rubric defines it as clarity, structure, and feasibility of translating ideas into actionable proposals Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 4.22 (SD 0.411) vs AI M 3.67 (SD 0.471); t(31) = 8.330, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 1.47, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Problem framing (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Task-specific rating of clarity in defining and focusing the design problem; anchors also address alignment with real-world needs (p. 9, Table 1; S1 Appendix, Problem framing). Three independent experts rated submitted ideation-process materials using five-level anchors; scores were averaged within participant and criterion before paired tests. Raters were blind to participant identity but not fully blind to condition. Holm correction covered the six ideation criteria; Cohen's dz is an absolute magnitude (pp. 8–12, Expert evaluation and Statistical analysis; S1 Appendix). Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 2.94 (SD 0.571) vs AI M 4.64 (SD 0.518); t(31) = -14.032, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 2.48, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Mechanism (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Expert-rated breadth and diversity of one participant's ideation strategies and ideas, including movement beyond conventional frameworks and cross-domain perspectives (p. 9, Table 1; S1 Appendix, Mechanism). Coded as within-person flexibility, not diversity across different people; no category count or between-person similarity measure was used. Three independent experts rated submitted ideation-process materials using five-level anchors; scores were averaged within participant and criterion before paired tests. Raters were blind to participant identity but not fully blind to condition. Holm correction covered the six ideation criteria; Cohen's dz is an absolute magnitude (pp. 8–12, Expert evaluation and Statistical analysis; S1 Appendix). Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 2.99 (SD 0.427) vs AI M 4.48 (SD 0.535); t(31) = -14.077, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 2.49, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Evaluator perspective (expert rating of ideation output)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Task-specific rating of visible comparison, selection, and justification of ideas; scoring anchors address systematic comparison, integration, and logical reasoning in submitted materials (p. 9, Table 1; S1 Appendix, Evaluator perspective). Three independent experts rated submitted ideation-process materials using five-level anchors; scores were averaged within participant and criterion before paired tests. Raters were blind to participant identity but not fully blind to condition. Holm correction covered the six ideation criteria; Cohen's dz is an absolute magnitude (pp. 8–12, Expert evaluation and Statistical analysis; S1 Appendix). Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 3.26 (SD 0.553) vs AI M 4.25 (SD 0.501); t(31) = -8.646, p < .001, Cohen's dz = 1.53, Holm-adjusted p < .001

outcomes.name: Form (expert rating of concept sheet)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Design-quality rating of structural clarity, proportion, and visual coherence; the full rubric also includes creativity of form, fluency of lines, and consistency with aesthetic and functional requirements (p. 9, Table 2; S2 Appendix, Form). Three independent experts rated standardized final concept sheets using five-level anchors; scores were averaged within participant and attribute before paired tests, using 32 participant-matched pairs (64 sheets total). Raters were blind to participant identity but not fully blind to condition. Holm correction covered the five design attributes; Cohen's dz is an absolute magnitude (pp. 6, 8–12; S2 Appendix). The concepts and selected visuals were generated during ideation with AI available; no new AI content was generated during concept-sheet assembly, but previously generated Midjourney images could be retained. Thus the rated sheets incorporate AI-assisted production across stages (pp. 6, 8–9; S4 Appendix, sections 4–5). Exploratory comparisons of participant-level AI-minus-human differences between the two sequence groups, including Mann–Whitney sensitivity analyses, found no significant order differences; carryover was not ruled out (p. 13, Reliability and preliminary analyses; S5 Appendix, Tables S5.2–S5.3).

contrasts.reported: Human M 4.08 (SD 0.406) vs AI M 4.11 (SD 0.375); t(31) = -0.325, p = .748, Cohen's dz = 0.06, Holm-adjusted p = .748

eligibility.reason: 32 people analyzed across both conditions (p. 5; t(31) in Tables 5-7), below 50. Criterion 1 also fails: the condition order was assigned by participant number and the paper states it was balanced but not randomized (p. 5), so this is a non-randomized within-person comparison. Expert ratings of the ideation output meet criterion 3. List in the screening report as a small, non-randomized experiment.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT-4o and Midjourney, 32 design students received higher expert ratings for creator perspective (originality; 4.03 vs 3.55, dz = 0.90) but lower ratings for innovation (3.40 vs 4.66, dz = 2.69) and proposed solution strategies (3.67 vs 4.22, dz = 1.47) than when working without AI (p. 14, Table 5).
notes: Fix review covered the complete markdown conversion through the references, PDF pages 1–18 and the supporting-information list on p. 22, and all five separately linked publisher DOCX appendices read in memory. All reported outcome statistics were checked against PDF Tables 5–6. The dataset URL was extracted from the PDF; the dataset was not downloaded or reanalyzed. Concept-sheet ratings concern the same AI-assisted concepts and retained generated visuals, with no new generation at assembly; mixed availability records that production-stage distinction rather than an independent unassisted post-AI task. The questionnaire measures are self-reports and are not included as output-scored outcomes. Cohen's dz values are the paper's absolute magnitudes (p. 12); effect direction is recorded separately.
